title: Chapter 6 Review & Practice Test
overview: Pull the whole chapter together: exponential functions and their inverses, logarithms, transformations, the power law and change of base, and logarithmic scales. Work through the summary, then use the review questions — taken from the chapter review and practice test and rewritten as full written and problem-solving questions — to check you are ready.
objectives: Connect exponential and logarithmic functions as inverses and compare their key features.
Graph and analyse transformed logarithmic functions.
Solve exponential equations with the power law and change of base formula.
Solve problems involving logarithmic scales and exponential models.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 at a glance
lessons.body:
Everything in this chapter grows from one idea: **the logarithm is the inverse of the exponential.**

| Section | Big idea | Key tool |
|---|---|---|
| 6.1 | $y = b^x$ grows by a constant factor; its rate of change is proportional to itself | finite differences, secant slopes, reflection in $y = x$ |
| 6.2 | $\log_b x$ is the exponent that turns $b$ into $x$ | $\log_b x = y \iff b^y = x$ |
| 6.3 | Logarithmic graphs transform like any other function | $f(x) = a\log[k(x - d)] + c$, anchor points $(1, 0)$, $(10, 1)$ |
| 6.4 | Exponents can be brought down to solve for them | $\log_b x^n = n\log_b x$, $\log_b m = \frac{\log m}{\log b}$ |
| 6.5 | Huge ranges are measured with log scales | pH, decibels, Richter, stellar magnitude |

```plot
title: The central picture of the chapter
f: 2^x | label=y = 2^x
f: logb(2, x) | label=y = log₂ x
f: x | dashed
domain: -4, 8
range: -4, 8
points: (0,1), (1,0), (1,2), (2,1)
```

lessons.title: Exponential vs logarithmic: the feature swap
lessons.body:
Because the graphs are reflections in $y = x$, every feature swaps roles:

| Feature | $y = b^x$ | $y = \log_b x$ |
|---|---|---|
| Domain | all reals | $x > 0$ |
| Range | $y > 0$ | all reals |
| Intercept | $y$-intercept 1 | $x$-intercept 1 |
| Asymptote | horizontal $y = 0$ | vertical $x = 0$ |
| Point with input 1 | $(1, b)$ | $(b, 1)$ |
| Rate of change | grows without bound ($b > 1$) | shrinks toward 0 ($b > 1$) |

If you remember one graph, you can always reconstruct the other.

lessons.title: Choosing a strategy
lessons.body:
**"Evaluate"** — rewrite the argument as a power of the base ($\log_2 \frac18 = -3$); use $\log_b b^k = k$; otherwise use change of base.

**"Solve for an exponent"** — isolate the power, take common logs, use the power law: $b^x = m \Rightarrow x = \frac{\log m}{\log b}$.

**"Solve a log equation"** — isolate the log and rewrite in exponential form: $\log_3 x = 4 \Rightarrow x = 81$.

**"Graph / key features"** — put in the form $a\log[k(x - d)] + c$, track $(1, 0)$, $(10, 1)$ and the asymptote $x = d$; domain from argument $> 0$.

**"Compare on a log scale"** — subtract the scale values, then rewrite as a power of 10 (taking account of any coefficient, e.g. 10 for decibels).

**Always check reasonableness:** $\log_5 17$ should lie between 1 and 2 because $5 < 17 < 25$.

lessons.title: Applications recap
lessons.body:
| Situation | Model | Typical question |
|---|---|---|
| Investment at rate $i$ per year | $A = P(1 + i)^t$ | doubling time $t = \frac{\log 2}{\log(1 + i)}$ |
| Depreciation, decay | $V = V_0(1 - r)^t$ | when is it worth half? |
| Light through glass or water | $I = I_0(0.8)^x$, $I = 100(0.39)^d$ | thickness/depth for a given intensity |
| Acidity | pH $= -\log[\text{H}^+]$ | pH ↔ concentration |
| Sound | $\beta_2 - \beta_1 = 10\log\frac{I_2}{I_1}$ | how many times as intense? |
| Earthquakes | $M = \log\frac{I}{I_0}$ | compare two quakes: $10^{M_2 - M_1}$ |

keyTerms.definition: $y = \log_b x$, the inverse of $y = b^x$; defined for $x > 0$.
A scale in which each unit represents multiplication by a constant factor.
$(1, 0)$ and $(10, 1)$ on $y = \log x$, used to sketch transformations.

workedExamples.title: Transformations and the inverse
workedExamples.problem: For $g(x) = 2\log(-x - 3) + 6$, describe the transformations, state the domain, range and asymptote, and identify the type of the inverse function.
steps: Factor: $-x - 3 = -(x + 3)$, so $g(x) = 2\log[-(x + 3)] + 6$: vertical stretch by 2, reflection in the $y$-axis, translation 3 left and 6 up.
Argument $> 0$: $-(x + 3) > 0 \Rightarrow x < -3$. Domain $x < -3$, range all reals, asymptote $x = -3$.

Anchor points: $(1, 0) \to (-4, 6)$ and $(10, 1) \to (-13, 8)$.
```plot
f: 2*log(-x-3) + 6
domain: -16, -2
range: -4, 10
points: (-4,6), (-13,8)
asymptote x: -3
```
The inverse of a logarithmic function is an **exponential** function: $x = 2\log[-(y + 3)] + 6 \Rightarrow y = -10^{(x - 6)/2} - 3$.
workedExamples.answer: Domain $x < -3$, asymptote $x = -3$; the inverse is exponential.

workedExamples.title: Doubling time
workedExamples.problem: 250 dollars is put in an account paying 6.5% compounded annually. How long until it doubles?

workedExamples.title: Sunlight under water
workedExamples.problem: The intensity of sunlight at depth $d$ metres is $I(d) = 100(0.39)^d$. Find the intensity at 3 m and the depth where it is 1 unit.
workedExamples.answer: About 5.9 units at 3 m; 1 unit at about 4.9 m.

workedExamples.title: Comparing pH values
workedExamples.problem: Chemical A has pH 6 and chemical B has pH 8. Compare their hydronium ion concentrations.
workedExamples.answer: Chemical A has 100 times the hydronium concentration of B.

misconceptions.fact: The inverse is $y = \log_b x$ (reflection in $y = x$); $\frac{1}{b^x} = b^{-x}$ is a reflection in the $y$-axis.
It shifts right 3; the asymptote is $x = 3$.
$\log 0.01 = -2$; only the argument must be positive.

realWorld.title: Space travel
realWorld.body: The chapter problem: radiation shielding ($P = 100(0.2)^x$), braking near a space station ($t = \log_{0.5}\frac{d}{1000}$) and star brightness all rely on exponentials and logarithms.

realWorld.title: Nuclear decay
realWorld.body: Stars are powered by nuclear reactions, and radioactive amounts follow $N(t) = N_0\left(\frac12\right)^{t/h}$ where $h$ is the half-life; logarithms find $t$ or $h$.

realWorld.title: Finance
realWorld.body: Banks, car dealers and investors use doubling times and depreciation times every day.

practice.question: State the domain, range and asymptote of $y = 3\log(-x)$.
How many times as intense is a 118 dB power saw as 85 dB traffic?

summary: The logarithmic function $y = \log_b x$ is the inverse of $y = b^x$; their key features swap.
Convert between forms with $\log_b x = y \iff b^y = x$; evaluate by writing arguments as powers.
Transform $y = \log x$ to $a\log[k(x - d)] + c$ using anchor points and the asymptote $x = d$.
Solve for unknown exponents with the power law; use change of base for any base.
Logarithmic scales (pH, dB, Richter) turn ratios into differences: each unit is a constant factor.

questions.text: Consider $f(x) = {{b}}^x$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the key features of $f$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how to graph $f^{-1}$ and give three points on it.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the key features of $f^{-1}$.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $f$: domain all reals; range $y > 0$; no $x$-intercept; $y$-intercept 1; positive for all $x$; increasing for all $x$; horizontal asymptote $y = 0$. Points $(-1, \tfrac{1}{ {{b}} })$, $(0, 1)$, $(1, {{b}})$.

(b) The inverse $f^{-1}(x) = \log_{ {{b}} } x$ is the reflection in $y = x$, through $(\tfrac{1}{ {{b}} }, -1)$, $(1, 0)$, $({{b}}, 1)$.

(c) $f^{-1}$: domain $x > 0$; range all reals; $x$-intercept 1; no $y$-intercept; negative for $0 < x < 1$, positive for $x > 1$; increasing; vertical asymptote $x = 0$.

rubric.point: Describes the inverse as the reflection in y = x with points
Correct key features of the inverse

questions.text: The graph of $y = \left(\frac{1}{ {{b}} }\right)^x$ passes through $(-1, {{b}})$, $(0, 1)$ and $(1, \tfrac{1}{ {{b}} })$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three points on the inverse and write its equation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the shape and key features of the inverse.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that the inverse can be written as $y = -\log_{ {{b}} } x$ and explain how this accounts for its shape.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Swap the coordinates: $({{b}}, -1)$, $(1, 0)$, $(\tfrac{1}{ {{b}} }, 1)$. The inverse is $y = \log_{1/{{b}}} x$ (or $x = \left(\frac{1}{ {{b}} }\right)^y$).

(b) The inverse is decreasing, has domain $x > 0$, range all reals, $x$-intercept 1 and vertical asymptote $x = 0$. It is positive for $0 < x < 1$ and negative for $x > 1$.

(c) Using change of base, $\log_{1/{{b}}} x = \frac{\log x}{\log(1/{{b}})} = -\frac{\log x}{\log {{b}}} = -\log_{ {{b}} } x$, so the inverse is the reflection of $y = \log_{ {{b}} } x$ in the $x$-axis — which is why it decreases.

rubric.point: Shows the inverse equals −log_b x using change of base

questions.text: Rewrite each equation in logarithmic form. Where an unknown appears in an exponent, solve for it.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $4^3 = 64 \Rightarrow \log_4 64 = 3$.

(b) ${{n}} = 3^x \Rightarrow x = \log_3 {{n}} = \frac{\log {{n}}}{\log 3} \approx {{log(n)/log(3):4}}$.

(c) $6^3 = y \Rightarrow \log_6 y = 3$ (and $y = 216$).

(d) $512 = 2^9 \Rightarrow \log_2 512 = 9$.

questions.text: Rewrite each equation in exponential form and solve for the unknown.

parts.label: b
parts.text: $x = \log_b 1$

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) ${{k}} = \log_2 x \Rightarrow x = 2^{ {{k}} } = {{2^k}}$.

(b) $x = \log_b 1 \Rightarrow b^x = 1 \Rightarrow x = 0$ (for any valid base).

(c) ${{j}} = \log_3 x \Rightarrow x = 3^{ {{j}} } = {{3^j}}$.

(d) $2 = \log_b {{c^2}} \Rightarrow b^2 = {{c^2}} \Rightarrow b = {{c}}$ (base must be positive).

rubric.point: (d) correct and rejects the negative base

questions.text: Estimate the value of $\log_2 {{n}}$ without using a calculator. Justify your estimate with mathematical reasoning, then check it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give your estimate to one decimal place.

questions.modelAnswer:
$2^{ {{floor(logb(2,n))}} } = {{2^floor(logb(2,n))}}$ and $2^{ {{floor(logb(2,n))+1}} } = {{2^(floor(logb(2,n))+1)}}$. Since ${{2^floor(logb(2,n))}} < {{n}} < {{2^(floor(logb(2,n))+1)}}$, the logarithm is between {{floor(logb(2,n))}} and {{floor(logb(2,n))+1}}.

Because exponential growth speeds up, ${{n}}$ being about {{(n - 2^floor(logb(2,n)))/2^floor(logb(2,n)):2}} of the way through the doubling suggests an exponent a little beyond a linear estimate. A reasonable estimate is about {{logb(2,n):2}}.

Check with the change of base formula: $\log_2 {{n}} = \frac{\log {{n}}}{\log 2} \approx {{logb(2,n):4}}$.

rubric.point: Brackets the value between consecutive powers of 2
Gives a reasonable estimate with justification
Checks with change of base or exponential form

questions.text: Evaluate each logarithm without a calculator.
Consider $y = -\log(x - {{d}}) + {{c}}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to graph the function using transformations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the domain, range and asymptote.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the $x$-intercept.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Reflect $y = \log x$ in the $x$-axis, translate {{d}} right and {{c}} up. Anchor points: $(1, 0) \to ({{1+d}}, {{c}})$ and $(10, 1) \to ({{10+d}}, {{c-1}})$.

(b) Domain $\{x > {{d}}\}$; range all reals; asymptote $x = {{d}}$.

(c) $x$-intercept: $\log(x - {{d}}) = {{c}} \Rightarrow x = 10^{ {{c}} } + {{d}} = {{10^c + d}}$.

questions.text: Consider $y = {{a}}\log(-x)$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the transformations and give the images of the anchor points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the domain, range and asymptote.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the intercepts and the value of $y$ when $x = -100$.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Reflect $y = \log x$ in the $y$-axis and stretch vertically by {{a}}: $(1, 0) \to (-1, 0)$, $(10, 1) \to (-10, {{a}})$.

(b) Domain $x < 0$; range all reals; asymptote $x = 0$.

(c) The $x$-intercept is $-1$ (from $-x = 1$); there is no $y$-intercept since $\log 0$ is undefined. At $x = -100$: $y = {{a}}\log 100 = {{2*a}}$.

rubric.point: Correct intercepts and value at x = −100

questions.text: Create a logarithmic function that is the result of applying **all** of these transformations to $y = \log x$: a horizontal stretch, a translation to the left, a vertical translation and a reflection. Then analyse your function.
questions.modelAnswer:
Sample: $y = \log\left[-\frac13(x + 2)\right] - 4$.

* $k = -\frac13$: horizontal stretch by 3 and reflection in the $y$-axis
* $d = -2$: translation 2 left; $c = -4$: translation 4 down

Anchor points: $(1, 0) \to (-3 - 2, -4) = (-5, -4)$; $(10, 1) \to (-30 - 2, -3) = (-32, -3)$.

Domain: $-\frac13(x + 2) > 0 \Rightarrow x < -2$; range all reals; asymptote $x = -2$.

(Any correct function with $|k| < 1$, $d < 0$, $c \neq 0$ and a reflection, with consistent features, earns full marks.)

rubric.point: Includes a left translation and a vertical translation

questions.text: Evaluate each expression using the power law of logarithms.
Solve for $x$, correct to three decimal places.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $x = \log_3 {{n}} = \frac{\log {{n}}}{\log 3} \approx {{log(n)/log(3):4}}$.

(b) $x = \log_2 0.{{z}} = \frac{\log 0.{{z}}}{\log 2} \approx {{log(z/100)/log(2):4}}$ (negative because $0.{{z}} < 1$).

(c) ${{b}}^x = {{m}} \Rightarrow x = \frac{\log {{m}}}{\log {{b}}} \approx {{log(m)/log(b):4}}$.

(d) ${{f}} = 100({{r}})^x \Rightarrow {{f/100}} = {{r}}^x \Rightarrow x = \frac{\log {{f/100}}}{\log {{r}}} \approx {{log(f/100)/log(r):4}}$.

questions.text: The intensity of light, in lumens, passing through glass $x$ millimetres thick is $I(x) = I_0({{r}})^x$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How thick should the glass be to block {{blk}}% of the light?

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the intensity changes as the glass gets thicker.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Blocking {{blk}}% leaves {{100 - blk}}%: ${{(100-blk)/100}} = {{r}}^x \Rightarrow x = \frac{\log {{(100-blk)/100}}}{\log {{r}}} \approx {{log((100-blk)/100)/log(r):3}}$ mm.

(b) Each millimetre multiplies the intensity by {{r}}, i.e. blocks {{100 - 100*r}}% of the light that reaches it. After $x$ mm the fraction transmitted is ${{r}}^x$, which decreases exponentially.

rubric.point: Correct equation using the fraction transmitted
Explains the exponential decrease per millimetre

questions.text: Explain how to sketch $y = \log_{ {{b}} } x$ without using technology, and how you could check your sketch with a graphing calculator.
questions.modelAnswer:
Graph $y = {{b}}^x$ using points $(-1, \tfrac{1}{ {{b}} })$, $(0, 1)$, $(1, {{b}})$, $(2, {{b^2}})$ and its asymptote $y = 0$. Reflect in $y = x$ by swapping coordinates: $(\tfrac{1}{ {{b}} }, -1)$, $(1, 0)$, $({{b}}, 1)$, $({{b^2}}, 2)$, with asymptote $x = 0$. Join with a smooth increasing curve that hugs $x = 0$ as $y$ becomes very negative.

To check, use the change of base formula and enter $y = \frac{\log x}{\log {{b}}}$ into the calculator.

rubric.point: Describes a valid technology check (change of base)

questions.text: Chemical A has a pH of {{pa}}, while chemical B has a pH of {{pb}}.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the hydronium ion concentration of each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How many times as great is the concentration in A as in B?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Classify each chemical.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $[\text{H}^+]_A = 10^{-{{pa}} }$ and $[\text{H}^+]_B = 10^{-{{pb}} }$.

(b) $\frac{[\text{H}^+]_A}{[\text{H}^+]_B} = 10^{ {{pb}} - {{pa}} } = 10^{ {{pb - pa}} } = {{10^(pb - pa)}}$. Chemical A has {{10^(pb - pa)}} times the hydronium ion concentration of chemical B.

(c) A is acidic (pH < 7); B is alkaline (pH > 7).

rubric.point: Correct ratio from the pH difference

questions.text: A magnitude {{m1}} earthquake and a magnitude {{m2}} earthquake are compared using $M = \log\left(\dfrac{I}{I_0}\right)$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many times as intense is the larger earthquake?

questions.modelAnswer:
$\frac{I_1}{I_2} = 10^{ {{m1}} - {{m2}} } = 10^{ {{m1 - m2:2}} } \approx {{10^(m1 - m2):3}}$.

The magnitude {{m1}} earthquake is about {{10^(m1 - m2):3}} times as intense — far more than the ratio of the magnitudes, ${{m1/m2:3}}$, because each unit on the Richter scale represents a factor of 10.

rubric.point: Explains why the magnitude ratio is misleading

questions.text: Welders use the shade number $n = 1 - \dfrac{7\log T}{3}$, where $T$ is the fraction of visible light the glass transmits.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What shade number transmits $\frac{1}{ {{q}} }$ of the light?

parts.label: b
parts.text: How does the shade number change when the transmitted fraction is divided by 10?

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the domain and range of this function in context.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $T = \frac{1}{ {{q}} }$: $n = 1 - \frac{7\log(1/{{q}})}{3} = 1 + \frac{7\log {{q}}}{3} \approx {{1 + 7*log(q)/3:3}}$.

(b) If $T$ is divided by 10, $\log T$ decreases by 1, so $n$ increases by $\frac{7}{3} \approx 2.33$. Each increase of about 2.3 in shade number means the glass lets through one tenth as much light.

(c) Domain: $0 < T \le 1$ (a fraction of the light). Range: $n \ge 1$ (when $T = 1$, $n = 1$; as $T \to 0$, $n$ increases without bound).

rubric.point: Explains the effect of dividing T by 10
Correct domain and range with reasoning

questions.text: Describe the graph of the inverse of $y = \left(\frac12\right)^x$, without drawing it.
questions.modelAnswer:
$y = (\frac12)^x$ passes through $(-2, 4)$, $(-1, 2)$, $(0, 1)$, $(1, \tfrac12)$ and has asymptote $y = 0$; it is decreasing.

Its inverse, $y = \log_{1/2} x$, passes through $(4, -2)$, $(2, -1)$, $(1, 0)$, $(\tfrac12, 1)$. It has domain $x > 0$, range all reals, vertical asymptote $x = 0$ and is **decreasing**: it starts high near the positive $y$-axis, crosses the $x$-axis at 1, and falls slowly to the right.

rubric.point: Correct domain, range and asymptote of the inverse
States the inverse is decreasing with correct description

questions.text: Describe the graph of $y = \log(x + {{h}}) - {{c}}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the $x$-intercept.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the $y$-intercept.

questions.modelAnswer:
Translate $y = \log x$ {{h}} units left and {{c}} units down.

* Anchor points: $(1, 0) \to ({{1 - h}}, -{{c}})$, $(10, 1) \to ({{10 - h}}, {{1 - c}})$
* Asymptote $x = -{{h}}$; domain $x > -{{h}}$; range all reals
* $x$-intercept: $\log(x + {{h}}) = {{c}} \Rightarrow x = 10^{ {{c}} } - {{h}} = {{10^c - h}}$
* $y$-intercept: $y = \log {{h}} - {{c}} \approx {{log(h) - c:3}}$

questions.text: Evaluate, correct to three decimal places.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $\log_6 {{m}} = \frac{\log {{m}}}{\log 6} \approx {{log(m)/log(6):4}}$.

(b) $\log_{12} {{n}} = \frac{\log {{n}}}{\log 12} \approx {{log(n)/log(12):4}}$.

Both are reasonable: e.g. $6^{ {{floor(log(m)/log(6))}} } < {{m}} < 6^{ {{floor(log(m)/log(6)) + 1}} }$.

questions.text: Consider $g(x) = 2\log(-x - {{h}}) + {{c}}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the transformations that map $f(x) = \log x$ onto $g$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the domain, range and asymptote.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find an equation for $g^{-1}$. What type of function is it?

parts.label: d
parts.text: Evaluate $g^{-1}({{c}})$.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Factor: $-x - {{h}} = -(x + {{h}})$, so $g(x) = 2\log[-(x + {{h}})] + {{c}}$: vertical stretch by 2, reflection in the $y$-axis, translation {{h}} left and {{c}} up.

(b) $-(x + {{h}}) > 0 \Rightarrow x < -{{h}}$. Domain $x < -{{h}}$; range all reals; asymptote $x = -{{h}}$. Anchor points: $(1, 0) \to ({{-1 - h}}, {{c}})$, $(10, 1) \to ({{-10 - h}}, {{2 + c}})$.

(c) Inverse: $x = 2\log[-(y + {{h}})] + {{c}} \Rightarrow \frac{x - {{c}}}{2} = \log[-(y + {{h}})] \Rightarrow -(y + {{h}}) = 10^{(x - {{c}})/2} \Rightarrow y = -10^{(x - {{c}})/2} - {{h}}$. The inverse is an exponential function (reflected in the $x$-axis and shifted).

(d) $g^{-1}({{c}}) = -10^0 - {{h}} = {{-1 - h}}$. Check: $g({{-1 - h}}) = 2\log 1 + {{c}} = {{c}}$ ✓.

rubric.point: Correct domain, asymptote and anchor points

questions.text: {{p}} dollars is put into an account paying {{r}}% interest, compounded annually.

parts.label: a
parts.text: How long will it take for the amount to double?

questions.modelAnswer:
$A = {{p}}({{g}})^t$. Double: ${{2*p}} = {{p}}({{g}})^t \Rightarrow 2 = {{g}}^t$.

$t = \frac{\log 2}{\log {{g}}} \approx {{log(2)/log(g):3}}$ years.

The principal cancels, so the doubling time does not depend on the {{p}} dollars invested.

rubric.point: Isolates the power and takes logs

questions.text: A solution has a pH of {{p}}. It is diluted so that its hydronium ion concentration is divided by {{k}}.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the original hydronium ion concentration.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the new pH.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the pH did not increase by the same factor.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Original $[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-{{p}} } \approx {{10^(-p):3}}$ mol/L.

(b) New concentration $= \frac{10^{-{{p}} }}{ {{k}} }$. New pH $= -\log\left(\frac{10^{-{{p}} }}{ {{k}} }\right) = {{p}} + \log {{k}} \approx {{p + log(k):3}}$.

(c) Dividing the concentration by {{k}} increases the pH by $\log {{k}} \approx {{log(k):3}}$, not by {{k}}: the pH scale is logarithmic. The solution becomes less acidic.

rubric.point: Explains the pH change as log k

questions.text: The intensity of sunlight decreases with depth $d$, in metres, below the surface of the ocean according to $I(d) = 100(0.39)^d$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is the intensity at a depth of {{d1}} m?

parts.label: b
parts.text: At what depth is the intensity {{q}} units?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what the base 0.39 tells you about the light.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $I({{d1}}) = 100(0.39)^{ {{d1}} } \approx {{100*0.39^d1:3}}$ units.

(b) ${{q}} = 100(0.39)^d \Rightarrow {{q/100}} = 0.39^d \Rightarrow d = \frac{\log {{q/100}}}{\log 0.39} \approx {{log(q/100)/log(0.39):3}}$ m.

(c) Every metre of depth multiplies the intensity by 0.39, so 61% of the remaining light is lost per metre; the intensity approaches 0 but never reaches it.

rubric.point: Correct intensity at the given depth
Isolates the power and solves with logs

questions.text: Consider $y = \log({{k}}x - {{m}})$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the domain, range, intercepts and asymptote.

parts.label: b
parts.text: How would the graph of $y = -\log({{k}}x - {{m}})$ differ?

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Factor: $y = \log[{{k}}(x - {{m/k:3}})]$: horizontal compression by $\frac{1}{ {{k}} }$ and translation {{m/k:3}} right.

Domain $x > {{m/k:3}}$; range all reals; asymptote $x = {{m/k:3}}$; $x$-intercept: ${{k}}x - {{m}} = 1 \Rightarrow x = {{(m+1)/k:3}}$; no $y$-intercept (argument negative at $x = 0$).

(b) $y = -\log({{k}}x - {{m}})$ is the reflection of this graph in the $x$-axis: same domain, asymptote and $x$-intercept, but it is decreasing instead of increasing (and positive for ${{m/k:3}} < x < {{(m+1)/k:3}}$).

rubric.point: Correct comparison with the reflected graph

questions.text: Design a method, using graphing technology, to demonstrate that the power law of logarithms, $\log x^n = n\log x$, holds. Use examples of your choice.
questions.modelAnswer:
Sample method:

1. Choose $n = 3$. Graph $Y_1 = \log(x^3)$ and $Y_2 = 3\log(x)$ on the same axes.
2. Observe that for $x > 0$ the graphs coincide (one lies exactly on top of the other).
3. Use the table feature: at $x = 2$, $Y_1 = \log 8 \approx 0.903$ and $Y_2 = 3\log 2 \approx 0.903$; at $x = 50$, both are about 5.097.
4. Repeat with other exponents, including a fraction ($n = \frac12$) and a negative number ($n = -2$).
5. Note the limitation: for $n = 2$, $\log(x^2)$ is also defined for $x < 0$ while $2\log x$ is not, so the graphs agree only for $x > 0$, which is the restriction in the power law.

questions.text: The slopes of tangents to $y = 2^x$ and $y = \log_2 x$ are compared at corresponding points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Estimate the slope of the tangent to $y = 2^x$ at $x = {{a}}$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Estimate the slope of the tangent to $y = \log_2 x$ at the corresponding point.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What is the relationship between the two slopes? Explain why.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) At $x = {{a}}$ on $y = 2^x$ (point $({{a}}, {{2^a}})$): slope $\approx \frac{2^{ {{a}}.001} - 2^{ {{a}} }}{0.001} \approx {{(2^(a+0.001) - 2^a)/0.001:3}}$.

(b) The corresponding point on $y = \log_2 x$ is $({{2^a}}, {{a}})$. Slope $\approx \frac{\log_2({{2^a}} + 0.001) - {{a}}}{0.001} \approx {{(logb(2, 2^a + 0.001) - a)/0.001:3}}$.

(c) The product of the slopes is about {{(2^(a+0.001) - 2^a)/0.001 * (logb(2, 2^a + 0.001) - a)/0.001:3}} ≈ 1: the slopes are reciprocals. Reflecting a line in $y = x$ swaps rise and run, so a tangent with slope $m$ becomes a tangent with slope $\frac1m$. This explains why the exponential's rate of change grows while the logarithm's shrinks.
